name: Upper brachial plexus palsy (Erb–Duchenne)
presentation: After a difficult delivery with shoulder dystocia, or a motorcycle crash in which the shoulder was forced down while the head went the other way, the arm hangs limp at the side, rotated inward with the elbow straight and the forearm pronated, the wrist and fingers flexed: the 'waiter's tip'. The hand grips normally. Sensation is reduced over the outer shoulder and the lateral forearm, and the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes are absent.

deficits.distribution: shoulder abductors and external rotators, elbow flexors, supinator
deficits.sign: Weak deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis; arm adducted, internally rotated, extended and pronated
Sensory loss over the deltoid and radial forearm
Hand and finger function preserved (C8–T1 intact)

reasoning: Forcing the head and shoulder apart stretches the upper part of the brachial plexus, the C5 and C6 roots and the upper trunk they form, while the lower roots are protected by their more horizontal course. The upper trunk gives the suprascapular nerve to the supraspinatus and infraspinatus, and its fibers continue into the lateral cord to the musculocutaneous nerve for the elbow flexors and into the posterior cord to the axillary nerve for the deltoid and teres minor; C5–C6 fibers also reach the brachioradialis and supinator through the radial nerve. Their loss paralyzes shoulder abduction and external rotation, elbow flexion and supination, and the intact antagonists supplied by C7–T1 pull the limb into the characteriztic adducted, internally rotated, extended and pronated posture. The C5 and C6 dermatomes cover the lateral shoulder, arm and forearm, so the sensory loss follows them, and the biceps and brachioradialis reflex arcs, which run through C5–C6, are lost while the C7 triceps jerk survives. The lesion is peripheral and uncrossed, so everything is ipsilateral. Whether the roots are avulsed from the cord (preganglionic, no recovery possible, with a Horner if T1 is also torn) or the trunk is stretched (postganglionic, recovery possible) is the crucial prognostic question: preserved sensory nerve action potentials in an anesthetic area show that the dorsal root ganglion is still connected to the periphery and the lesion is preganglionic.

imagingFindings.finding: Edema and T2 hyperintensity of the C5–C6 roots and upper trunk on MR neurography; pseudomeningoceles at the foramina indicate root avulsion.
CT myelography showing contrast-filled pseudomeningoceles and absent rootlets at C5–C6.
Denervation in C5–C6 muscles with preserved lateral antebrachial cutaneous sensory responses in avulsion (preganglionic) or absent responses in trunk lesions (postganglionic).

mimics.name: C5–C6 radiculopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Neck pain, usually one root, paraspinal denervation

mimics.name: Rotator cuff tear
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pain and weakness of abduction without sensory loss or reflex change

management: Physiotherapy to prevent contractures; most obstetric palsies recover within months
EMG at 3–4 weeks and MRI to define avulsion; nerve grafting or transfers if no biceps recovery by 3–6 months
Late tendon transfers for fixed deficits

imagingHint.label: upper trunk of the brachial plexus
